candidate_relations.reason: Toxic epidermal necrolysis is the same diagnostic object as the reference for ciprofloxacin-triggered generalized bullae with mucosal erosions.
Anemia is a laboratory finding, not toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Marked transaminase and bilirubin elevation is associated liver injury, not the cutaneous TEN diagnosis.
Severe cutaneous adverse reaction is the parent class and omits TEN as the specific grade.
Cholestatic jaundice accompanies the drug reaction but is not TEN.
Stevens–Johnson syndrome is the related milder SCAR grade, not TEN.
AGEP is a distinct pustular SCAR, not widespread bullae with mucosal erosions.
Viral hepatitis does not explain ciprofloxacin-timed generalized bullae and mucosal erosions.
Drug-induced SJS/TEN correctly implicates ciprofloxacin but does not commit to TEN versus SJS.
Drug-induced liver injury with skin manifestations makes the hepatitis primary rather than TEN with hepatic involvement.
Erythema multiforme is a related but distinct, typically more limited acral/mucosal eruption.
Severe drug eruption is a compatible parent without TEN specificity.
INR 2.7 and bilirubin 14 mg/dL indicate associated liver failure physiology, not the TEN diagnosis.
Drug-induced hypersensitivity syndrome/DRESS is a distinct SCAR with different timing and organ pattern.
DRESS is incompatible with this acute bullous mucosal eruption two days after ciprofloxacin.
Sepsis does not account for the drug-timed bullous mucocutaneous eruption.
Wilson disease is not supported and does not explain the bullous drug eruption.
Framing the case as DILI with skin findings conflicts with TEN as the primary diagnostic object.
The eruption began two days after ciprofloxacin, so an infection-caused SCAR conflicts with the drug etiology.
Infectious mononucleosis is not suggested by this bullous drug eruption.

case_quality_flags: BSA and Nikolsky sign not recorded; concurrent cholestatic liver injury
